items.titleTr: Increase in direct cremations since pandemic
items.summaryTr: A 2026 Cost of Dying Report found direct cremation was now chosen for around one in five funerals.
items.articleText: Increase in direct cremations since pandemic - Published Funeral directors say there has been an increase in direct cremations, with no mourners in attendance, since the Covid-19 pandemic. Brian Ugalde, whose firm of funeral directors has worked in Cornwall for 135 years, said non-attendance had become more acceptable since the lockdowns when families were not always allowed to attend. He said: "A funeral is a ceremony...a farewell, a celebration... it is for for those left behind," he said. But, he said, direct cremation came after Covid when "the model became acceptable and practical", as well as being cheaper. SunLife's 2026 Cost of Dying Report found direct cremation was now chosen for around one in five funerals in the UK. The report said, in the majority of cases, the deceased had requested or arranged a direct cremation themselves before their death. In 86% of those cases, families decided to hold their own celebration of their loved one's life at a later occasion. Andrew Judd from The Association of Funeral Directors said families did not always realise exactly what was included when they bought a direct cremation plan. "The average cost of a direct cremation at the moment is £1,628," he said. "So that's the cost of the person that you've lost being collected from where they died, being cremated somewhere in the country and you having the ashes delivered back to you, that's all it is." If you were to have an attended funeral service, that can range from £4,200, but you have a funeral with that." John Ware from Walter C Parsons funeral directors in Plympton suggested people talked to loved ones before buying an unattended cremation plan so their family knew what to expect. "If they talk to their local funeral director there is probably an option that sits somewhere between a direct cremation and a completely traditional funeral which would suit the need of both parties, in terms of keeping the cost lower, but also having a service that the family can attend to reflect on that person's life." Plymouth's The Park crematorium, which opened in 2024, has recently reduced the cost of direct cremation, citing lower prices offered by other crematoria and national companies. Graham Smith, head of bereavement, registration and coroner services at Plymouth City Council, said national providers could use crematoria in other parts of the country meaning not everyone was cremated in their home city. "In my view if you live in Plymouth, if you work in Plymouth, why would you use a national provider?" VAT, the cost of wood for coffins and fuel price increases have all added to the cost of traditional funeral services. But people the BBC spoke to in Plymouth had mixed views on direct cremation. Andrew Statton said he had not previously heard of direct cremation but added: "My wife died seven years ago of cancer and we had the ashes and then had a memorial service afterwards, so it makes no difference does it?" Ann Roberts said she would consider a direct cremation because it would save her family money and they could "decide what they want to do". She added: "If you don't talk to your family, they won't know what you want." But Pam Brinkhurst said she preferred a more tradition funeral. "When you get cremated or buried the family are there. It's a much better send off." Phoenix Elson agreed: "I would rather pay the extra money and for my son to actually be there to celebrate my life". Simplicity is one of the national companies offering direct cremation and said "our nationwide network of crematoria helps us keep fees competitive". They added: "Giving customers more choice, including the option to be cremated locally rather than having their loved one transported across the country to secure the lowest fee, is a positive development for consumers and the sector as a whole in the Plymouth area." items.titleTr: Gilts v kilts: What is happening with Scottish government bonds?
items.summaryTr: MSPs have heard both the pros and cons of the government's plan to launch its first ever bond to the market.
items.articleText: Gilts v kilts: What is happening with Scottish government bonds? - Published The Scottish government is facing questions about its plan to issue its first ever bonds. The move would allow ministers to borrow money from investors who in return receive regular interest payments. The aim is to raise about £1.5bn by the end of the parliamentary term, with the funds to be used on long-term projects such as building hospitals or maintaining roads. Named "kilts", a nod to UK government "gilts", the scheme has provoked much debate. This week, MSPs on Holyrood's finance committee heard about the potential risks and rewards. What are bonds? A bond is a financial tool used by a government to borrow money. They are sold with a promise for the buyer, or investor, to be paid back at the end of an agreed term. The government will also make regular payments to the investor. In the UK, a government bond is called a gilt. They are typically bought by financial institutions such as pension funds, insurance companies and commercial banks. As a play on this term, the Scottish bonds have been nicknamed "kilts". When will the 'kilts' be launched? The Scottish government has said it expects the bonds to be issued within this financial year, subject to market conditions. Former First Minister Humza Yousaf commissioned initial work in 2023 after advisers in the Scottish government's investor panel recommended making bonds available to the market as a means of raising Scotland's profile and attracting investment. In November last year, the government announced that it had received an identical credit rating to the UK's score. This was based on "prudent fiscal management" and the country's economic stability - though ministers were warned this could change if Scotland moved towards independence. With market volatility due to conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, some have questioned whether now is a good time to launch bonds. But at Holyrood, David McMillan, professor in finance and accounting at the University of Stirling, told MSPs: "You can't wait for a perfect time because there's going to be no perfect time." How much could they raise? The government wants to raise £1.5bn through bonds by 2031, although that would only be a fraction of its near £70bn budget. About four-fifths of the Scottish government's budget is used on resource spending, which goes towards day-to-day costs such as funding the NHS, benefits payments and paying salaries. A smaller portion is made up of capital spending, typically used on long-term physical assets such as buildings and bridges, or maintaining roads or paths. The Scottish government is unable to borrow for resource spending other than to correct forecasting errors. However, for capital spending, it can borrow as much as £450m a year at 2023-24 levels up to a total cap of £3bn - to be uprated with inflation. Adjusted for inflation, the government could borrow about £491m in the current financial year, with a total limit of about £3.3bn. What are the pros and cons? Economists have noted that Scottish bonds would be a more costly way of borrowing than existing routes provided by the UK government through the National Loans Fund. It has been estimated, external that interest rates on "kilts" would be 0.3 percentage points above gilts, plus an additional £2m per bond in administrative costs. The Scottish government has not released costings, citing market sensitivities, but has insisted, external issuing bonds would represent value for money relative to the costs of borrowing through the UK scheme. Ministers argue that issuing bonds would be a good opportunity to market the country to investors, and would be helpful if Scotland became independent. Dr Ben Cormier, a senior lecturer at the University of Strathclyde's department of government and public policy, told Holyrood's finance committee that while the Scottish bonds could cost marginally more than the UK scheme, they would "bring flexibility to public finances and debt management". McMillan agreed with the plans "in principle", but warned they would lose "credibility" with investors if limited to five years. Cormier warned that independence was the one thing "that could materially change the nature of risk associated with Scottish bonds". Conservative MSP Liam Kerr said bonds could be more expensive than borrowing through the National Loans Fund and voiced concerns about a lack of transparency in the programme. McMillan agreed there should be "full information" available, saying: "You've got to have a clear, full and frank conversation with the public."
